BEGINNERS · TECHNIQUE

Classification: What Your Screen Separates—and What It Doesn’t

By the Old-Timer · Published October 7, 2026

The Old-Timer is Gold Trails’ editorial voice. Content assembled with assistance from ChatGPT. Sources are linked throughout.

A classifier looks like a simple sieve, and that is a good place to begin. Its useful job is to divide material by size. It does not look at a grain and decide whether it is worth keeping.

Once you understand that distinction, screening becomes easier to plan—and easier to describe in a sample log.

The short version

  • A screen separates by size, not by value.
  • Keep the retained and passing material identifiable.
  • Record the opening and whether input was measured before or after screening.
  • Check oversized material before deciding what to discard.

Two fractions, two responsibilities

The Forest Service and BLM booklet describes a grizzly above a gold pan: finer material passes through while larger rocks remain. It also calls for checking the oversized material for nuggets and washing clay from cobbles. Gold Panning · 2018 revisionU.S. Forest Service & BLMPrinted pages 9–11 · PDF pages 13–15Describes a grizzly separating larger rocks, checking oversize for nuggets, and washing clay from cobbles.View original source ↗Opens another website in a new tab; this article stays open.

The practical implication is simple: “too large to pass through” is not the same as “contains no gold.” You have created a retained fraction and a passing fraction. Keep track of both until you have made the checks appropriate to your material.

Do not call the passing material “all the gold” or the retained material “waste” just because it sits above the screen. Those names assume a result that the screen has not established.

Write down the actual opening

For your notebook, record the screen opening and its unit as specified for your screen. A useful entry is more precise than “fine classifier” or “the small screen.” If a label is unclear, consult the maker’s specification rather than guessing.

There is no single opening recommended here for every river, every gold size, and every piece of recovery equipment. Choose a screening approach for the material and method you are using, then describe it accurately. A detailed note is more helpful than borrowing someone else’s screen choice without knowing their conditions.

The booklet’s example is regional recreational guidance. Treat it as an illustration of the process, rather than a universal equipment prescription.

A manageable working routine

Our suggested routine is to label the sample first, arrange a stable receiving container, and work with an amount you can handle without spilling. Keep the two size fractions identifiable while you examine and process them.

If you use water while screening, keep the receiving arrangement under control so you know where the passing material went. If material spills, note the loss. A spill does not become unimportant just because it happened before panning.

Keep enough space to see what you are doing. When tired, cold, or rushed, reducing the batch is a reasonable choice. Processing more gravel is not useful if you lose track of the sample.

Measure on the same side of the screen

A scoop measured before screening and a scoop measured afterward describe different inputs. The first includes the material later retained above the screen; the second describes only the passing fraction.

For a comparison between sample locations, choose which input you will measure and keep that convention consistent. Write it down alongside the amount, unit, and opening. If you change the convention, mark the change so later results are not mistaken for directly comparable ones.

This is our recordkeeping recommendation, not a professional sampling standard. For the larger routine and a downloadable notebook, see How to Compare Test Pans Without Fooling Yourself.

Know what screening has accomplished

At the end, you should be able to say what material passed, what remained, and what you did with each. That is a useful result even before a flake appears in the pan.

Screening prepares material; it does not establish recovery, identification, or the value of a deposit. Those questions still need their own observations. If a yellow particle is part of the next step, read Is That Really Gold? before recording it as confirmed gold.

Look up classification, classifier, and recovery in the glossary.

Sources and scope

  1. Gold Panning · 2018 revision. U.S. Forest Service & BLM. Printed pages 9–11; PDF pages 13–15.
